Photograph: Richard Wainwright/EPA England cricket team Moeen Ali warns England ‘cannot win the World Cup’ by sidelining Adil Rashid
 Leg-spinner made one appearance in recent tri-series
 Liam Dawson has retained place in Australia
 Ali Martin in Hobart Mon 16 Nov 2026 06.09 EST Last modified on Tue 17 Nov 2026 00.10 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Adil Rashid has become a slightly peripheral figure in England’s white-ball plans this winter, with his close friend Moeen Ali now openly criticising the ­management and warning it could damage their World Cup chances next year. After a hand injury at the end of the home summer, Rashid made one low-key outing during the recent tri-series in Pakistan. While he began the Australia tour with figures of four for 35 in the warm-up match in Perth, Liam Dawson has remained the chosen spinner for the first two one-day internationals.
 Harry Brook, the captain, claimed the initial preference for Dawson in Perth was down to the conditions encountered and a more all-round game that lengthens the batting. His continuation on a flatter surface in Adelaide raised more eyebrows, even if the move to leave out Jamie Overton did risk a longer tail without him.
 Banton’s century leads England to emphatic win in second ODI amid Australian soap opera Read more Moeen is not convinced and puts last month’s failure to defend 429 against Sri Lanka – plus the record 89-run 10th-wicket stand that allowed Pakistan to pull off a similarly stunning heist three days later – squarely down to the selection call. His concern is that Rashid is being eased out of the side.
 “England cannot win the World Cup next year without Rash in the team,” he said. “And sorry, they would not have lost those two games in Pakistan with him playing either. When Jos Buttler was in bad form a while back they didn’t drop him. Why? Because we know he’s one of our best players and a match-winner. Same goes for Rash. He has been world-class over many years.”
 Moeen’s close bond with Rashid should be taken into account, but it may also hint at how the leg-spinner – England’s leading white-ball wicket-taker with a combined 415 scalps and world champion in both formats – is feeling.
 Rashid is not one to rock the boat, but the situation feels unlikely to change come Wednesday’s ODI decider at Hobart’s Bellerive Oval. After three relatively frugal outings in the otherwise run-soaked tri-series, Dawson shut down half-centuries from Matt Renshaw and Cameron Green during Sunday’s march to a 135-run win .
 View image in fullscreen Liam Dawson took two wickets in England’s decisive victory in the second game of the ODI series against Australia. Photograph: Mark Brake/Cricket Australia/Getty Images As Moeen notes, Rashid has not been in prime form this year and took one wicket in the three ODIs he played against India during the summer. Though a mainstay in the XI for more than a decade, he will turn 39 in February. Brook has publicly praised Rashid on this tour, calling him “a magician with the ball” who can “tear through sides”. But for all that, and with a year to run on his central contract, there has been a broader sense that belief in Rashid has been on the wane under Brook and ­Brendon McCullum, the head coach.
 Rashid has sent down his full allocation in just five of the 16 ODIs he has played since Brook became full-time captain in April last year and in none of his last four T20is. This would have been inconceivable under Brook’s predecessors, with one of them, ­Buttler, recently making a similar point to Moeen on his podcast.

 “For us as a team to win that World Cup, Adil Rashid has to be there and be near his best,” said Buttler during his current absence after hamstring surgery last month. “No slight on anybody else, there isn’t another Adil Rashid.”
 Beyond recent form, another ­factor is said to be Dawson’s greater tactical input in a side that, beyond Joe Root, is light on 50-over nous. While far less experienced than Rashid at international level – and at 36, just two years younger – he has played 179 List A games since his debut for Hampshire in 2007.
 After swapping South Australia for Tasmania on Monday, England have one training day to get used to a new set of conditions. The series decider is also likely to mean a reunion with Mahli Beardman, the 21-year-old quick who ran through them with six wickets on debut in Perth before being rested for the second match.
